mode: anguilliform undulatory giant, toothed apex predator, low tail fin, no dorsal fin
note: Sander et al. 2021 (Science) reconstruct a 17.65 m, ~44.7 t basal-plan anguilliform giant; cruise follows the Watanabe et al. 2015 mass^0.20 allometry at shark-like k=0.5, and burst the Bainbridge/Wardle fast-start scaling (U ~ 4·L^-0.5 BL/s), which predicts under 1 BL/s at whale scale.

mode: subcarangiform undulatory, deep-chested shastasaurid, pod-forming toothed apex predator
note: Kelley et al. 2022 (Curr. Biol.) confirm robust cutting teeth in adults and a deeper-than-1970s-reconstruction ribcage at 13.5-15 m; cruise/burst use the same whale-scale allometric estimate as Cymbospondylus, discounted slightly for the heavier shastasaurid trunk.

mode: paraxial forelimb paddle rowing for a slow search, trunk/tail undulation for the fast strike
note: Klein et al. 2022 and Krahl 2021's functional analysis of paraxial nothosauroid swimming give two gears - slow forelimb 'flying-rowing' and a fast tail-undulation strike; cruise scaled from sea-lion paddle-rowing, burst from shark-like undulatory allometry.

mode: long-bodied undulation with limb paddling, ambush lurker with a reach-around-corners neck
note: Spiekman et al. 2024 read it as a non-pursuit ambusher that keeps its bulky body out of prey's sight; cruise/burst are the shark-like allometric estimate discounted for a body built for concealment rather than speed.

mode: thunniform-ish cruiser, fusiform holocephalan body, lunate tail, no pelvic fins
note: Tapanila & Pruitt 2013's fusiform, lunate-tailed eugeneodont reconstruction (whorl aside) reads as a lamnid-shark analogue; cruise/burst follow the mako allometry of Nosal et al. 2024, and like any shark it never backs up.

mode: four-flipper synchronized underwater flight, tail for steering only
note: Wintrich et al. 2017 compare the four-flipper stroke of the first known plesiosaur to penguins and sea turtles; cruise/burst scale that flight-swimming analogue down from penguin cruising speed by body length.

mode: slow bottom-grazing paddler, hammerhead scrape-and-filter feeder
note: Chun et al. 2016 describe a slow bottom-grazer scraping algae with hammerhead jaws then sieving it out the sides; cruise/burst follow a dugong/manatee grazing-swimmer analogue at this body length.

mode: anguilliform tail-driven swimmer, limbs reduced to steering only
note: Müller 2005 and the 2024 thalattosaur review read the 60-plus-vertebra tail as the main propulsor; cruise/burst are the eel-like allometric estimate for a flexible axial swimmer of this length.

mode: negatively buoyant benthic bottom-walker with a slow tail scull
note: Neenan's Fossil Focus reads Placodus as a ballasted seabed walker with pachyostotic bone and a gastral basket; speeds follow a manatee-like benthic-grazer analogue, near the bottom of the roster.

mode: carangiform generalist shark, moderate cruiser with spine-braced fins
note: A generalist Muschelkalk hybodont with no dedicated kinematic study; cruise/burst follow a modern generalist-shark analogue (nurse/Port Jackson shark cruise), and like any shark it does not back up.

mode: thunniform pursuit predator, naked tuna-shaped body, wide-gape lunge
note: Romano et al. 2017 describe a scaleless, deeply forked-tail apex predator among Triassic actinopterygians; cruise/burst follow the mako/tuna cruising-predator analogue (Nosal et al. 2024) at the upper end of thunniform cruise.

mode: elongate anguilliform amphibian, lateral-line-guided ambush with a sideways jaw swipe
note: NHM Oslo's Svalbard temnospondyl work describes a lateral-line-guided ambush predator in a nearshore shelf deposit; cruise/burst are the cold-blooded amphibian allometric estimate for an elongate body of this length.

mode: carangiform axial swimmer stabilized by a soft-tissue dorsal fin, flipper-assisted steering
note: Renesto et al. 2020 read the dorsal fin and caudal lobe as adaptations for stable, sustained undulatory swimming, more fish-like than other early ichthyosaurs; cruise/burst are the small-agile-swimmer allometric estimate.

mode: sluggish benthic paddler, square armoured shell as ballast
note: Pommery et al. 2021 describe weak limbs under a heavy fused-plate shell; speeds follow a sea-turtle/manatee lower bound as the slowest swimmer on the roster.

mode: needlefish ambush, motionless drift then a single fast-start dash
note: Kogan et al. 2015's flow-tank/CFD work shows pike-like low-disturbance fast starts; cruise is near zero (a drifting ambusher) and burst follows the Bainbridge fast-start scaling for a slender fish of this size.

mode: armoured, toothless pelican-style pouch-gulper, slow benthopelagic swimmer
note: Motani, Pyenson & Jiang 2025 favour a pelican-like gulp-feeder over the earlier baleen-filter hypothesis; cruise/burst are the armoured-benthic allometric estimate for a stiff-trunked, plate-backed swimmer.

mode: forelimb-driven rowing with tail-assisted turns, hatchling-tier shoaling pachypleurosaur
note: Xue et al. 2015 describe a broad, forelimb-dominant propulsive limb and pachyostotic ballast ribs; cruise/burst are the small-agile-swimmer allometric estimate for the commonest reptile of the Xingyi fauna.

mode: flexible-wristed benthic swimmer in shallow flats, ballast ribs
note: Motani et al. 2014 describe cartilage-rich, sea-turtle-flipper-like wrists and pachyostotic ribs built for shallow water; speeds follow a sea-turtle-hatchling crawl-swim analogue.

mode: slow benthic-swimming early turtle with a ventral plastron shell
note: Li et al. 2008 describe unspecialised limbs and no paddles on a nearshore stem turtle; speeds follow a sea-turtle-hatchling benthic-swimmer analogue.

mode: jet (funnel), aperture-backward primary, buoyant chambered shell
note: Nautilus analogue measured directly: 0.35-1.6 BL/s, mean ~0.9 BL/s backward (Neil & Askew 2018); the ceratitic shell sits in the same low-drag Westermann morphospace as living Nautilus at matching scale.

mode: jet-propelled coleoid with a three-lobed fin sheet, hook-armed grappler, omnidirectional escape
note: The Polzberg soft-tissue material (ink sac, arm hooks, pro-ostracum) reads as a squid-like jet swimmer; cruise/burst follow a modern small-coleoid jet analogue, backward through the funnel as the fast escape direction.

mode: stiff-necked bank ambusher, minimal swimmer, hindlimb-driven bursts in the shallows
note: Renesto & Saller 2018 and Spiekman et al. 2020 read it as shore-based with only short hindlimb-driven swimming bursts in shallow water, not a pursuit swimmer; values are nominal since it rarely leaves the bank.

mode: crocodile-like surface tail-sculling ambusher, slow in open water
note: Butler et al. 2019 document marine-lagoon phytosaurs with crocodile-like proportions; cruise/burst follow a crocodilian surface-ambush analogue, slow except for the lunge.

mode: terrestrial shore runner, negligible swimmer
note: Miedema et al. 2020 describe a fast terrestrial runner found in marine rock only by wash-in; swim values are nominal since it does not enter open water.

mode: terrestrial theropod, does not swim
note: An optional Late Triassic estuary visitor with no aquatic adaptations; swim values are a nominal placeholder since it never enters the water.
